```{python}
#| label: setup
# This page only reads the summary files made by scripts/12-summarize_results.py and shows them; no analysis here.
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import polars as pl
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

from senate_forecast_2026.paths import SUMMARY_DATA
from senate_forecast_2026.queries import CHART_START, ELECTION_DAY, STATE_NAMES
from senate_forecast_2026.schemas import (AGE_GROUPS, EDUCATION, GENDERS, IDEOLOGIES, INCOMES, MARITAL_STATUSES,
                                          PARTY_IDS, RACES, REGISTERED, RELIGIONS, SEXUALITIES, VOTES_2024)
from senate_forecast_2026.website import (DEM, INK, MUTED, REP, choice_menu, choices, colour_of, coloured_share,
                                          figure_html, folded, interval, last_name, pct, show, split_bar, table)


def read(name):
    return pl.read_parquet(SUMMARY_DATA / f"{name}.parquet")


control = read("forecast_control")
comparison = read("control_comparison")
# The combined forecast's chance of Democratic control with the 2024 voters (the forecast) and the 2022 midterm's.
turnout_control = dict(read("turnout_comparison").select("turnout", "dem_control").rows())
# One model's full run: its cost, from the price check of the most expensive models and from our own run.
price_estimates = read("price_estimates")
full_run_cost = dict(price_estimates.select("model", "full_run_cost").rows())
full_run_calls = price_estimates["full_run_calls"][0]
# What each model's full run actually cost (the costs table), for the models not in price_estimates.
run_cost = dict(read("costs").filter(pl.col("model") != "all models").select("model", "total_cost").rows())
seats = read("forecast_seats")
races = read("forecast_races")
models = read("models")

NUMBER_WORDS = {2: "two", 3: "three", 4: "four", 5: "five", 6: "six", 7: "seven", 8: "eight", 9: "nine", 10: "ten"}


def one_in(chance):
    """A chance in words, from "one-in-two" to "one-in-ten": 0.24 is "one-in-four" (1 / 0.24 is about 4).
    Chances above about 67% still say one-in-two, and below about 10% one-in-ten."""
    return f"one-in-{NUMBER_WORDS[min(max(round(1 / chance), 2), 10)]}"


def model_name(model, name=None):
    """How a model is named on the page: its ID (or a given short name), with a maple leaf for Cohere, which is
    Canadian."""
    name = name or model
    return f"{name} 🍁" if model.startswith("cohere/") else name


# Numbers quoted in the text: the combined forecast (every model), and the models behind it.
combined = control.filter(pl.col("version_type") == "all").row(0, named=True)
model_ids = models["model"].unique().sort().to_list()
model_list = ", ".join(model_name(m) for m in model_ids[:-1]) + " and " + model_name(model_ids[-1])

# The versions of the results, as the forecast has them: every model together ("all"), each approach, each model.
VERSION_ORDER = {"all": 0, "approach": 1, "model": 2}
VERSIONS = control.sort(pl.col("version_type").replace_strict(VERSION_ORDER), "version").select(
    "version_type", "version").rows()


def version_label(version_type, version):
    return {"all": "All models combined", "approach": f"{version.title()}'s approach"}.get(version_type,
                                                                                            model_name(version))


# Models better known by their maker's name than their own ("Command" alone means little).
SHORT_MODEL_NAMES = {"cohere/command-a-plus": "Cohere"}


def short_version(version_type, version):
    """A short name for chart labels: "All", the approach, or the model's name without provider or version."""
    if version_type != "model":
        return {"all": "All", "approach": version.title()}[version_type]
    return model_name(version, SHORT_MODEL_NAMES.get(version, version.split("/")[-1].split("-")[0].title()))


def models_of(version_type, version):
    """The models behind a version."""
    if version_type == "all":
        return models["model"].to_list()
    if version_type == "approach":
        return models.filter(pl.col("approach") == version)["model"].to_list()
    return [version]


def by_version(build):
    """One view per version, switched by the version menu at the top of the page. `build(version_type, version)`
    makes each view's HTML."""
    return choices("version", {version_label(*v): build(*v) for v in VERSIONS}, picker=False)


# The persona variables, in the order of their categories in the CES.
VARIABLES = {
    "gender": ("Gender", GENDERS), "race": ("Race", RACES), "age_group": ("Age", AGE_GROUPS),
    "education": ("Education", EDUCATION), "income": ("Income", INCOMES), "party_id": ("Party ID", PARTY_IDS),
    "ideology": ("Ideology", IDEOLOGIES), "religion": ("Religion", RELIGIONS),
    "marital_status": ("Marital status", MARITAL_STATUSES), "sexuality": ("Sexuality", SEXUALITIES),
    "registered": ("Registered to vote", REGISTERED), "vote_2024": ("2024 vote", VOTES_2024),
    "state": ("State", sorted(STATE_NAMES, key=STATE_NAMES.get)),  # in the order of the states' names
}


def in_order(groups, order):
    """`groups` in the CES order, with any not in it (e.g. "Missing") at the end."""
    return sorted(groups, key=lambda g: order.index(g) if g in order else len(order))


def short_names(candidates):
    """Each candidate's last name, or their full name when two candidates share a last name (Alaska's Sullivans)."""
    last_names = [last_name(c) for c in candidates]
    return {c: (c if last_names.count(last_name(c)) > 1 else last_name(c)) for c in candidates}


# Races ordered from the most Republican to the most Democratic in the combined forecast.
order = races.filter((pl.col("version") == "all") & (pl.col("party") == "Republican")).sort(
    "share", descending=True)["state"].to_list()

```

This page tests whether silicon sampling [@argyle2023], predicting votes using large language models (LLMs) and voter demographic information, can accurately predict the outcomes of elections. In this case, we are predicting all 35 Senate races and the chance that the Democrats get control of the US Senate in the election on November 3, 2026.

## Who controls the Senate? {#forecast data-kicker="The forecast"}

```{python}
#| label: headline
def headline(version_type, version):
    result = control.filter(pl.col("version") == version).row(0, named=True)
    return (
        '<div class="headline">'
        f'<div><div class="number" style="color:{DEM}">{pct(result["dem_control"])}</div>'
        '<div class="label">chance the Democrats control the Senate, from 10,000 simulated elections</div></div>'
        f'<div><div class="number">{result["seats"]:.0f} <span class="interval">'
        f'{interval(result["seats_lower"], result["seats_upper"])}</span></div>'
        '<div class="label">Democratic-caucus seats; 51 gives control</div></div></div>'
        '<div class="bar-label"><span>Chance of control</span><span>Democrats / Republicans</span></div>'
        + split_bar([(f"{pct(result['dem_control'])} Democrats", result["dem_control"], DEM),
                     (f"{pct(1 - result['dem_control'])} Republicans", 1 - result["dem_control"], REP)])
    )


show(by_version(headline))
```

Simulated votes were created with four models: `{python} model_list`. They were all given equal weight and a multilevel logistic regression was run on the outputs to get an average impact for each of the persona features: age group, gender, race, education, party ID and state. Those impact values were then used to simulate the votes for Senator in each of the 35 states using the voting population from the 2024 CES [@ces2024]. We then ran 10,000 simulations of the election using a normal distribution of a state error of `{python} pct(combined['state_error_sd'], 1)` (a polling error of `{python} pct(combined['polling_state_error_sd'])` combined with the model's own uncertainty of `{python} pct(combined['model_standard_error'], 1)`) and a national error of `{python} pct(combined['national_error_sd'])`. The results of our simulations and silicon samples give the Democrats a `{python} pct(combined['dem_control'])` chance of taking control of the Senate.

### How many seats

```{python}
#| label: seat-distribution
def seat_chart(version_type, version):
    rows = seats.filter(pl.col("version") == version).sort("dem_seats")
    figure = go.Figure(go.Bar(
        x=rows["dem_seats"], y=rows["share"], marker_color=[DEM if s >= 51 else REP for s in rows["dem_seats"]],
        marker_line_width=0, customdata=rows["simulations"],
        hovertemplate="<b>%{x} Democratic seats</b><br>%{y:.1%} of simulations (%{customdata:,})<extra></extra>",
    ))
    ticks = list(range(int(seats["dem_seats"].min()), int(seats["dem_seats"].max()) + 1, 2))
    figure.update_xaxes(tickvals=ticks, ticktext=[f"<span style='color:{DEM}'>{s}</span><br>"
                                                  f"<span style='color:{REP}'>{100 - s}</span>" for s in ticks])
    figure.update_yaxes(tickformat=".0%")
    figure.add_vline(x=50.5, line_dash="dot", line_color=INK, line_width=1)
    figure.add_annotation(x=50.5, y=1, yref="paper", text="51 seats: control", showarrow=False, xanchor="left",
                          xshift=6, font=dict(size=12, color=MUTED))
    return ('<p class="bar-label"><span></span><span>Democratic seats, with Republican seats in red below</span></p>'
            + figure_html(figure, 320))


show(by_version(seat_chart))
```

Shown above are the results of 10,000 simulations of the election based on our silicon samples. Each bar shows the share of the simulations that ended with that many seats. Bars in red represent Republicans maintaining control of the Senate, while bars in blue represent Democrats gaining control of the Senate. Along the bottom, each label shows the number of Democratic seats in blue, with the number of Republican seats in red below it. Note that in the case of 50 seats for each, control goes to the Republicans because the Republican Vice President has the deciding vote. The most likely result is `{python} int(combined['seats'])` Democratic seats and `{python} 100 - int(combined['seats'])` Republican seats, and 95% of the simulations had between `{python} int(combined['seats_lower'])` and `{python} int(combined['seats_upper'])` Democratic seats.

### Compared with other forecasts

```{python}
#| label: control-comparison
def day(date):
    return f"{date.day} {date:%B}"


OTHER_FORECASTS = {
    "polls": lambda date: f"The polls<br><span style='font-size:11px'>averages to {day(date)}</span>",
    "polymarket": lambda date: f"Polymarket<br><span style='font-size:11px'>{day(date)}</span>",
    "silver_bulletin": lambda date: f"Silver Bulletin<br><span style='font-size:11px'>{day(date)}</span>",
}


def comparison_chart():
    """Our combined forecast, each of our models alone (grey), and the other forecasts. The same for every version
    in the menu, so the models' spread is always shown."""
    ours = control.filter(pl.col("version_type") == "all")["dem_control"][0]
    by_model = control.filter(pl.col("version_type") == "model").sort("dem_control")
    labels = [f"<b style='color:{INK}'>Our forecast</b><br><span style='font-size:11px'>all models combined</span>",
              "Our models<br><span style='font-size:11px'>one at a time</span>"]
    labels += [OTHER_FORECASTS[row["source"]](row["date"]) for row in comparison.iter_rows(named=True)]
    others = comparison["dem_control"].to_list()
    figure = go.Figure([
        go.Scatter(x=[ours, *others], y=[labels[0], *labels[2:]], mode="markers+text",
                   text=[pct(c) for c in [ours, *others]], textposition="middle right",

                   marker=dict(size=[18, 13, 13, 13], color=[DEM, "white", "white", "white"],
                               line=dict(color=DEM, width=2.5))),
        go.Scatter(x=by_model["dem_control"], y=[labels[1]] * by_model.height, mode="markers+text",
                   text=[f"{short_version('model', m)} {pct(c)}" for m, c in by_model.select("version", "dem_control").rows()],
                   textposition="top center", textfont=dict(size=11, color=MUTED), cliponaxis=False,
                   customdata=[model_name(m) for m in by_model["version"]], hovertemplate="<b>%{customdata}</b><br>%{x:.0%}<extra></extra>",
                   marker=dict(size=10, color=MUTED)),
    ])
    figure.update_xaxes(range=[0, 1], tickvals=[0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1], tickformat=".0%")
    figure.update_yaxes(categoryorder="array", categoryarray=labels, autorange="reversed", showgrid=True,
                        ticklabelstandoff=10)
    figure.add_vline(x=0.5, line_dash="dot", line_color=INK, line_width=1)
    figure.add_annotation(x=0.5, y=1, yref="paper", yanchor="bottom", text="50%", showarrow=False,
                          font=dict(size=12, color=MUTED))
    figure.update_layout(margin=dict(t=24, r=40))
    return ('<p class="bar-label"><span></span><span>Chance the Democrats control the Senate</span></p>'
            + figure_html(figure, 320))


# Numbers quoted in the text below: the other forecasts, and our models' lowest and highest chance.
other_forecasts = dict(comparison.select("source", "dem_control").rows())
models_by_chance = control.filter(pl.col("version_type") == "model").sort("dem_control")
lowest_model, highest_model = models_by_chance.row(0, named=True), models_by_chance.row(-1, named=True)

show(comparison_chart())
```

Because silicon sampling is a recent technique, we compare it to other methods of predicting elections: polls [averages of the polls from @votehub, run through our simulation, with the 2024 presidential result for the 9 races without polls], betting markets [@polymarket], and professional forecasters [@silver_senate, subscription required]. The comparisons are updated daily until November 2, when the website will be frozen. Our forecast gives the Democrats a `{python} pct(combined['dem_control'])` chance of taking control of the Senate, which is lower than the polls at `{python} pct(other_forecasts['polls'])`, Polymarket at `{python} pct(other_forecasts['polymarket'])` and Silver Bulletin at `{python} pct(other_forecasts['silver_bulletin'])`. One reason they might differ is that the LLMs only know the persona, the candidates and what they learned in their training, and not the latest news and campaigns [such as Trump's historically low approval rating, see @silver_approval] that the polls, the betting markets and the forecasters can follow. The predictions from each of our four models are also shown, and they range from `{python} pct(lowest_model['dem_control'])` (`{python} short_version('model', lowest_model['version'])`) to `{python} pct(highest_model['dem_control'])` (`{python} short_version('model', highest_model['version'])`).

## Race by race: our forecast, the polls and Polymarket {#races data-kicker="The races"}

::: {.how-to-read}
**Leading vote share:** the share of the candidate ahead, in our forecast and in the latest poll average, coloured by
the leader's party. **95% interval:** for ours, from the simulated elections; for the polls, the average ± 1.96 times how
much the polls disagree with each other, where 95% of the polls would fall. **Chance of winning:** ours, from the
simulated elections, and Polymarket's latest price. Rows where the polls or Polymarket have a different leader from
ours are highlighted. Races are ordered from the most Republican to the most Democratic in the combined forecast.
:::

```{python}
#| label: races
def race_rows(state, candidates):
    """Two rows for one race. Leading vote share: ours and the latest poll average's, with their 95% interval. Chance of
    winning: ours and Polymarket's latest price."""
    who = " v ".join(f"{last_name(c['candidate'])} ({c['party'][0]})" for c in candidates.iter_rows(named=True))

    def chance(column):
        if candidates[column].null_count() > 0:
            return '<span class="muted">no market</span>'
        leader = candidates.sort(column, descending=True).row(0, named=True)
        bar = split_bar([(c["candidate"], c[column], colour_of(c["party"]))
                         for c in candidates.sort("party").iter_rows(named=True)], thin=True)
        return (f'<div class="chance-row">{bar}<span style="color:{colour_of(leader["party"])}">'
                f'{pct(leader[column])} {last_name(leader["candidate"])}</span></div>')

    def leader_share(candidate, share):
        return f'<b style="color:{colour_of(candidate["party"])}">{pct(share, 1)} {last_name(candidate["candidate"])}</b>'

    ours = candidates.sort("share", descending=True).row(0, named=True)
    ours_share = leader_share(ours, ours["share"])
    ours_uncertainty = interval(ours["share_lower"], ours["share_upper"], True, 1, label=False)
    polls_disagree = False
    if candidates["poll_average"].null_count() == candidates.height:
        polls_share, polls_uncertainty = '<span class="muted">no polls</span>', ""
    else:
        polls = candidates.sort("poll_average", descending=True, nulls_last=True).row(0, named=True)
        polls_share = leader_share(polls, polls["poll_average"])
        polls_uncertainty = interval(polls["poll_lower"], polls["poll_upper"], True, 1, label=False)
        polls_disagree = polls["candidate"] != ours["candidate"]
    our_favourite = candidates.sort("chance_of_winning", descending=True).row(0, named=True)
    market_disagree = (candidates["polymarket_chance"].null_count() == 0 and
                       candidates.sort("polymarket_chance", descending=True).row(0, named=True)["candidate"]
                       != our_favourite["candidate"])

    # Where the polls or Polymarket have a different leader from ours, their row is highlighted.
    flag = '<span class="flag">different leader</span>'
    polls_class = ' class="disagree"' if polls_disagree else ""
    market_class = ' class="disagree"' if market_disagree else ""
    race = (f'<td rowspan="2" class="race-cell"><div class="race-name">{STATE_NAMES[state]}</div>'
            f'<div class="race-who">{who}</div></td>')
    return (f'<tbody class="race">'
            f'<tr class="first">{race}<td class="source">Ours</td><td>{ours_share}</td>'
            f'<td class="muted">{ours_uncertainty}</td>'
            f'<td class="source">Ours</td><td>{chance("chance_of_winning")}</td></tr>'
            f'<tr class="last"><td class="source{" disagree" if polls_disagree else ""}">Polls</td>'
            f'<td{polls_class}>{polls_share}{flag if polls_disagree else ""}</td>'
            f'<td{polls_class}><span class="muted">{polls_uncertainty}</span></td>'
            f'<td class="source{" disagree" if market_disagree else ""}">Polymarket</td>'
            f'<td{market_class}>{chance("polymarket_chance")}{flag if market_disagree else ""}</td></tr></tbody>')


def race_table(version_type, version):
    version_races = races.filter(pl.col("version") == version)
    return (
        '<table class="plain races" data-quarto-disable-processing="true"><thead><tr>'
        '<th style="width:15%">Race</th><th style="width:8%"></th><th style="width:20%">Leading vote share</th>'
        '<th style="width:23%">95% interval</th><th style="width:11%"></th><th style="width:23%">Chance of winning</th>'
        "</tr></thead>"
        + "".join(race_rows(state, version_races.filter(pl.col("state") == state)) for state in order)
        + "</table>"
    )


show(by_version(race_table))
```

```{python}
#| label: races-numbers
# Numbers quoted in the text below, from the combined forecast: the races where the latest poll average or
# Polymarket has a different leader from ours, and how often our Republican share is above the polls'.
def listed(names):
    names = sorted(names)
    return names[0] if len(names) == 1 else ", ".join(names[:-1]) + " and " + names[-1]


combined_races = races.filter(pl.col("version") == "all")


def leaders(column):
    rows = combined_races.filter(pl.col(column).is_not_null()).sort(column, descending=True)
    return dict(rows.group_by("state", maintain_order=True).first().select("state", "candidate").rows())


our_leaders = leaders("share")
polls_differ = [STATE_NAMES[s] for s, c in leaders("poll_average").items() if c != our_leaders[s]]
market_differs = [STATE_NAMES[s] for s, c in leaders("polymarket_chance").items() if c != our_leaders[s]]
republicans_with_polls = combined_races.filter((pl.col("party") == "Republican") & pl.col("poll_average").is_not_null())
races_with_polls = republicans_with_polls.height
more_republican = republicans_with_polls.filter(pl.col("share") > pl.col("poll_average")).height
```

In our comparison with the polls and Polymarket, most of our results agree on who is ahead. The latest poll average has a different leader from ours in only `{python} len(polls_differ)` of the `{python} races_with_polls` races with polls (`{python} listed(polls_differ)`), and Polymarket in `{python} len(market_differs)` of 35 (`{python} listed(market_differs)`). In each of them, our forecast has the Republican narrowly ahead, while the others have the Democrat ahead. More generally, our forecast leans Republican compared with the polls: our Republican share is above the poll average in `{python} more_republican` of the `{python} races_with_polls` races with polls. As in the comparison of the forecasts, one likely reason is that the models have a political bias despite the prompting, or that they do not know this year's news and campaigns, which the polls and Polymarket follow. It is hard to identify the cause, since there are many parts of the method we cannot control. The actual election results may clarify some of this.

Our 95% intervals and the polls' intervals are not comparable, because they measure two different things. Ours comes from the simulated elections, so it includes the possible polling error and the model's own uncertainty (see [Uncertainty](#uncertainty)). The polls' interval only shows how much the polls of a race disagree with each other. It is not a margin of error, and the real result can fall outside it. The two intervals should be read with that in mind.

## The polls and Polymarket, race by race {#polls data-kicker="Polls & markets"}

::: {.how-to-read}
Pick a race. **Top:** the poll average over time (undecided left out) with the polls' 95% interval as a band; on the
right, our forecast of each candidate's share with its 95% interval, from all models combined and from each version.
**Bottom:** Polymarket's daily price for each candidate; on the right, our chance of winning. **Table:** the polls in
today's average, the most influential first.
:::

```{python}
#| label: polls-and-markets
rule_columns = [c for c in read("poll_averages").columns if c.startswith("by_")]
parties = races.filter(pl.col("version") == "all").select("state", "candidate", "party")
averages = read("poll_averages").filter(pl.all_horizontal(rule_columns)).join(parties, on=["state", "candidate"],
                                                                                  how="left")
prices = read("polymarket_prices").join(parties, on=["state", "candidate"], how="left")
poll_table = read("poll_table").join(parties, on=["state", "candidate"], how="left")


def end_labels(figure, lines, value_format):
    """Each line's name at its right end, nudged apart so that close lines' names do not overlap."""
    ends = sorted(lines, key=lambda line: line["y"])
    for lower, upper in zip(ends, ends[1:]):
        upper["label_y"] = max(upper["y"], lower.get("label_y", lower["y"]) + 0.045)
    for line in ends:
        figure.add_annotation(x=line["x"], y=line.get("label_y", line["y"]), xanchor="left", xshift=4, showarrow=False,
                              text=f"<b>{line['name']}</b> {value_format(line['y'])}",
                              font=dict(color=line["colour"], size=12), row=1, col=1)


def two_panels():
    """A chart over time on the left and our forecast on the right, side by side so they never overlap."""
    figure = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, shared_yaxes=True, column_widths=[0.62, 0.38], horizontal_spacing=0.06)
    figure.add_annotation(text="Our forecast", x=0.5, xref="x2 domain", y=1, yref="paper", yanchor="bottom", yshift=14,
                          showarrow=False, font=dict(size=12, color=MUTED))
    figure.update_layout(hovermode="closest", margin=dict(t=44))
    return figure


# Empty slots between one candidate's dots and the next's, wide enough for the combined forecast's number.
GAP_BETWEEN_CANDIDATES = 3


def forecast_panel(figure, forecasts, column, with_interval):
    """Our forecast for each candidate, from every version side by side (all models combined first): a dot (with its
    95% interval), the combined forecast's number to its left (every version's number is in its hover label), the
    versions' names slanted below and the candidate's name above their group."""
    names = short_names(forecasts["candidate"].unique().to_list())
    candidates = forecasts.filter(pl.col("version") == "all").sort("share", descending=True)["candidate"].to_list()
    positions, labels = [], []
    for i, candidate in enumerate(candidates):
        rows = forecasts.filter(pl.col("candidate") == candidate)
        colour = colour_of(rows["party"][0])
        for j, (version_type, version) in enumerate(VERSIONS):
            row = rows.filter(pl.col("version") == version).row(0, named=True)
            x, value = i * (len(VERSIONS) + GAP_BETWEEN_CANDIDATES) + j, row[column]
            positions.append(x)
            labels.append(short_version(version_type, version))
            error = (dict(type="data", symmetric=False, array=[row["share_upper"] - value],
                          arrayminus=[value - row["share_lower"]], color=colour, thickness=1.5, width=4)
                     if with_interval else None)
            detail = f" {interval(row['share_lower'], row['share_upper'], True, 1)}" if with_interval else ""
            is_combined = version_type == "all"
            figure.add_scatter(x=[x], y=[value], mode="markers+text" if is_combined else "markers", row=1, col=2,
                               error_y=error,
                               marker=dict(color=colour, size=9 if is_combined else 7,
                                           symbol="circle" if is_combined else "circle-open",
                                           line=dict(color=colour, width=1.5)),
                               text=[pct(value, 1 if with_interval else 0)] if is_combined else None,
                               textposition="middle left",
                               textfont=dict(color=colour, size=11),
                               hovertemplate=f"<b>{names[candidate]}</b>, {version_label(version_type, version)}: "
                               f"{pct(value, 1)}{detail}<extra></extra>")
        middle = i * (len(VERSIONS) + GAP_BETWEEN_CANDIDATES) + (len(VERSIONS) - 1) / 2
        figure.add_annotation(x=middle, y=1, xref="x2", yref="paper", yanchor="bottom", showarrow=False,
                              text=f"<b>{names[candidate]}</b>", font=dict(color=colour, size=12))
    figure.update_xaxes(tickvals=positions, ticktext=labels, tickangle=-60, tickfont=dict(size=10), automargin=True,
                        showline=False, ticks="", range=[-GAP_BETWEEN_CANDIDATES - 1.5, max(positions) + 1.5],
                        row=1, col=2)


def leave_room_for_labels(figure, last):
    """The time axis from CHART_START to election day, marked with a dotted line, and wider on the right if the names
    at the lines' ends need more room."""
    figure.update_xaxes(range=[CHART_START, max(ELECTION_DAY, last + (last - CHART_START) * 0.22)], row=1, col=1)
    figure.add_vline(x=ELECTION_DAY, line=dict(color=MUTED, width=1, dash="dot"), row=1, col=1)
    figure.add_annotation(x=ELECTION_DAY, y=1, xref="x", yref="paper", yanchor="bottom", showarrow=False,
                          text="Election day", font=dict(size=11, color=MUTED))


def polls_figure(state, rows):
    figure, ends, names = two_panels(), [], short_names(rows["candidate"].unique().to_list())
    for (candidate,), line in rows.sort("date").group_by("candidate", maintain_order=True):
        colour, name = colour_of(line["party"][0]), names[candidate]
        dates = line["date"].to_list()
        figure.add_scatter(x=dates + dates[::-1], hoverinfo="skip", line=dict(width=0), fill="toself",
                           fillcolor=colour, opacity=0.12, row=1, col=1,
                           y=line["upper"].to_list() + line["lower"].to_list()[::-1])
        figure.add_scatter(x=line["date"], y=line["average"], mode="lines", line=dict(color=colour, width=2.5),
                           customdata=line.select(pl.col("lower", "upper") * 100), row=1, col=1,
                           hovertemplate=f"<b>{name}</b> %{{x|%b %d}}: %{{y:.1%}} "
                           "[%{customdata[0]:.1f}, %{customdata[1]:.1f}] 95% interval<extra></extra>")
        ends.append({"x": dates[-1], "y": line["average"][-1], "name": name, "colour": colour})
    end_labels(figure, ends, lambda y: pct(y))
    leave_room_for_labels(figure, rows["date"].max())
    forecast_panel(figure, races.filter(pl.col("state") == state), "share", with_interval=True)
    figure.update_yaxes(tickformat=".0%")
    return figure_html(figure, 320)


def market_figure(state, rows):
    figure, ends, names = two_panels(), [], short_names(rows["candidate"].unique().to_list())
    for (candidate,), line in rows.sort("date").group_by("candidate", maintain_order=True):
        colour, name = colour_of(line["party"][0]), names[candidate]
        figure.add_scatter(x=line["date"], y=line["price"], mode="lines", line=dict(color=colour, width=2), row=1, col=1,
                           hovertemplate=f"<b>{candidate}</b> %{{x|%b %d}}: %{{y:.0%}}<extra></extra>")
        ends.append({"x": line["date"][-1], "y": line["price"][-1], "name": name, "colour": colour})
    end_labels(figure, ends, lambda y: pct(y))
    leave_room_for_labels(figure, rows["date"].max())
    forecast_panel(figure, races.filter(pl.col("state") == state), "chance_of_winning", with_interval=False)
    figure.update_yaxes(tickformat=".0%", range=[-0.02, 1.02])
    return figure_html(figure, 260)


POPULATIONS = {"Likely voters": "LV", "Registered voters": "RV", "Adults": "A"}


def polls_in_average(rows):
    """The table of polls under the charts: dates, pollster, sample, its weight in the average (with a bar), each
    candidate's share as the poll reported it, and the leader's lead."""
    names = short_names(rows["candidate"].unique().to_list())
    candidates = rows.group_by("candidate", "party").agg(pl.col("share").mean()).sort("share", descending=True)
    largest = rows["influence"].max()
    table_rows = []
    for (poll_id,), poll in rows.group_by("poll_id", maintain_order=True):
        first = poll.row(0, named=True)
        shares = dict(zip(poll["candidate"], poll["share"], strict=True))
        start, end = first["start_date"], first["date"]
        dates = f"{start:%b %-d}–{end:%b %-d}" if start != end else f"{end:%b %-d}"
        sample = (f'{first["sample_size"]:,}' if first["sample_size"] else "–") + \
            (f' {POPULATIONS.get(first["population"], "")}' if first["population"] else "")
        bar = (f'<div class="influence"><span style="width:{100 * first["influence"] / largest:.0f}%"></span>'
               f'<i>{first["influence"]:.2f}</i></div>')
        leader_party = candidates.filter(pl.col("candidate") == first["leader"])["party"]
        lead_colour = colour_of(leader_party[0]) if leader_party.len() else MUTED
        lead = ("Tie" if first["lead"] == 0 else
                f'<span style="color:{lead_colour}">{names.get(first["leader"], first["leader"])} '
                f'+{100 * first["lead"]:.0f}</span>')
        table_rows.append([dates, first["pollster"], sample, bar]
                          + [f'<span style="color:{colour_of(c["party"])}">{pct(shares[c["candidate"]])}</span>'
                             if c["candidate"] in shares else "–" for c in candidates.iter_rows(named=True)]
                          + [lead])
    headers = ["Dates", "Pollster", "Sample", "Influence", *[names[c] for c in candidates["candidate"]], "Lead"]
    return ('<p class="chart-title">Polls in today\'s average</p>'
            + table(headers, table_rows, numeric_from=4, css_class="polls-table"))


views = {}
for state in sorted(STATE_NAMES, key=STATE_NAMES.get):
    poll_rows, price_rows = averages.filter(pl.col("state") == state), prices.filter(pl.col("state") == state)
    content = '<p class="chart-title">Poll average</p>'
    content += polls_figure(state, poll_rows) if poll_rows.height else '<p class="muted">No polls for this race.</p>'
    content += '<p class="chart-title">Polymarket price</p>'
    content += (market_figure(state, price_rows) if price_rows.height
                else '<p class="muted">No market for this race.</p>')
    state_polls = poll_table.filter(pl.col("state") == state)
    content += polls_in_average(state_polls) if state_polls.height else ""
    views[STATE_NAMES[state]] = content
show(choices("state", views))
```

The poll average of a race is a weighted mean of the polls listed by VoteHub, with undecided voters left out so that the shares add up to 100%. Each poll's weight, which we call its influence in the table, comes from four rules:

1. It halves every 14 days after the poll finished.
2. It grows with the square root of the number of people asked (up to 5,000).
3. It is divided by the square root of the number of polls of the race from the same pollster in the last 60 days, so that no pollster dominates.
4. Polls of likely voters count fully, polls of registered voters 0.8 and polls of adults 0.6.

In simple terms, an influence of 1 is about what a new poll of 600 likely voters would get, from a pollster with no other recent poll of the race. The polls' 95% interval is the average ± 1.96 times the weighted spread of the polls around it. A Polymarket price is what traders pay for a share that pays $1 if the candidate wins, so a price of 70 cents can be read as a 70% chance of winning. We show the last price of each day.

## Compared with past elections {#past data-kicker="Past elections"}

::: {.how-to-read}
The Republican share of all votes in each state's recent elections, and our 2026 forecast with its 95% interval. Red
above 50%, blue below.
:::

```{python}
#| label: past-elections
past = read("past_comparison")
ELECTIONS = {"senate_2020": "Senate 2020", "senate_2022": "Senate 2022", "president_2024": "President 2024",
             "senate_2024_special": "Senate 2024 special"}


def past_table(version_type, version):
    rows = []
    for state in order:
        state_rows = past.filter((pl.col("state") == state)
                                 & (pl.col("version").is_null() | (pl.col("version") == version)))
        by_election = {r["election"]: r for r in state_rows.iter_rows(named=True)}
        ours = by_election["forecast_2026"]
        rows.append([STATE_NAMES[state]]
                    + [coloured_share(by_election[e]["republican_share"], 1) if e in by_election else ""
                       for e in ELECTIONS]
                    + [f'<b>{coloured_share(ours["republican_share"], 1)}</b><br>'
                       f'<span class="muted small">{interval(ours["lower"], ours["upper"], True, 1)}</span>'])
    return table(["State", *ELECTIONS.values(), "Our forecast, 2026"], rows)


show(by_version(past_table))
```

Our forecast is more Democratic than the 2024 presidential election in most states: our Republican share is below Trump's 2024 share in 31 of the 35 states, typically by 2.9 points. The largest moves towards the Democrats are in Delaware, Idaho, New Jersey and New Mexico. In Idaho and Nebraska, the Republican faces an independent rather than a Democrat, and the past results have no such race to compare with. The past shares are of all votes, minor candidates included, while ours are of our main candidates only, so ours are slightly higher for both sides than they would be with minor candidates. Midterm elections usually swing against the president's party, which would push the same way. Even so, our forecast gives the Democrats less than an even chance of control, because they need to win 17 of the 35 races, and 22 of the seats up this year are held by Republicans, most of them in states Trump won.

## What the models answered {#answers data-kicker="Model answers"}

::: {.how-to-read}
The weighted share of each answer. With all models combined (or an approach), each model is shown and then their
average, the models counted equally. The Senate question names the race's real candidates (grouped here by party);
the House question is a generic ballot asked as a benchmark, not used in the forecast.
:::

```{python}
#| label: model-answers
answers = read("model_answers")
ANSWER_ORDER = ["Democrat", "Independent", "Other", "Undecided", "Would not vote", "Republican"]
QUESTIONS = {"senate": "Senate: “Who will you vote for?”", "generic": "House: “Which party's candidate will you vote for?”"}


def answer_bars(version_type, version):
    shown = answers.filter(pl.col("model").is_in(models_of(version_type, version)) & (pl.col("version_type") == "model"))
    if version_type != "model":
        shown = pl.concat([shown, answers.filter(pl.col("version") == version)])
    pieces = ['<div class="legend">' + "".join(
        f'<span><span class="key" style="background:{colour_of(a)}"></span>{a}</span>' for a in ANSWER_ORDER) + "</div>"]
    for question, title in QUESTIONS.items():
        pieces.append(f"<h3>{title}</h3>")
        for (model,), rows in shown.filter(pl.col("question") == question).group_by("model", maintain_order=True):
            shares = dict(zip(rows["answer"], rows["share"], strict=True))
            pieces.append(f'<div class="bar-label"><span>{"Average of the models" if model == "average" else model_name(model)}'
                          f'</span><span>{pct(shares.get("Democrat", 0))} D / {pct(shares.get("Republican", 0))} R'
                          "</span></div>")
            pieces.append(split_bar([(pct(shares[a]), shares[a], colour_of(a)) for a in ANSWER_ORDER if a in shares]))
    return "".join(pieces)


show(by_version(answer_bars))
```

These bars show how the models answered across all 1,050 personas, weighted by their CES weights, before the forecast model adjusts the answers to each state's voters. On average across the four models, 40% of the answers to the Senate question were for the Republican, 34% for the Democrat and 3% for an independent; 7% were undecided and 15% would not vote. The House question gave a similar split, 41% Republican and 37% Democrat.

Jev 1.14, our only decision model, gave by far the most undecided answers (13%, against 1% to 7% for the others), and Kimi K3 the fewest. This may reflect the models' architectures, in the terms of Kahneman's [*Thinking, Fast and Slow*](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374533557/thinkingfastandslow). Jev 1.14 is what its makers call a "System One" model: it makes a fast, one-step judgement, picking from the options with a probability for each, and in such a quick judgement a persona's vote may not be settled. Our other three models, Kimi K3, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Command A+ 🍁, are closer to System Two: they write their answer out, and more reasoning can lead them to a decision. Jev 1.14's answers also varied the most from draw to draw: with 3 draws each, it gave the same answer all 3 times for 73% of personas, against 90% to 98% for the other models.

### Checks

::: {.how-to-read}
Two checks on 10 personas: does the model give the persona's own state when asked, and do its answers change
when party ID is left out of the prompt.
:::

```{python}
#| label: checks
CHECKS = {"persona_state": "Gives the persona's own state", "no_party_id": "Answer changes without party ID"}
check_results = read("check_results").sort("check", "model", descending=[True, False])
check_answers = read("check_answers").sort("check", "model", "persona_id", "question", "prompt")


def check_tables(version_type, version):
    chosen = models_of(version_type, version)
    results = check_results.filter(pl.col("model").is_in(chosen))
    details = check_answers.filter(pl.col("model").is_in(chosen))
    return (
        table(["Check", "Model", "Personas", "Cost"],
              [[CHECKS[r["check"]], model_name(r["model"]), f'{r["count"]} of {r["personas"]}', f'${r["cost"]:.4f}']
               for r in results.iter_rows(named=True)], numeric_from=2)
        + folded("Every answer in the checks", table(
            ["Check", "Model", "Persona", "State", "Party ID", "Question", "Prompt", "Answer", "Draws"],
            [[CHECKS[r["check"]], model_name(r["model"]), r["persona_id"], r["state"], r["party_id"], r["question"], r["prompt"],
              r["answer"], r["draws"]] for r in details.iter_rows(named=True)], numeric_from=8))
    )


show(by_version(check_tables))
```

Every model gave the persona's own state for all 10 personas, so we can confirm that they read the persona and do not just answer at random. With the party ID line taken out of the prompt, the most common answer changed on at least one of the questions (Senate, House or, in Alaska, the final round) for 1 (Kimi K3) to 4 (Claude Haiku 5.5) of the 10 personas. So party ID matters, but most answers did not depend on it alone: the rest of the persona, such as ideology, race and religion, carries much of the same information. Both checks, on 10 personas each, cost about $0.24 in all.

## Cross-tabs {#crosstabs data-kicker="Cross-tabs"}

::: {.how-to-read}
Each party's share of the answers for a party, in each group of personas: the Senate question (the race's Democratic,
independent or Republican candidate) and the House question (Democrat or Republican). Undecided and would-not-vote
answers are left out. With all models combined (or an approach), each model's share is worked out first and then
averaged, the models counted equally. Personas: how many answered for a party in that group (on the Senate question).
:::

```{python}
#| label: crosstabs
crosstabs = read("crosstabs")
COLUMNS = [("senate", "Democrat"), ("senate", "Independent"), ("senate", "Republican"),
           ("generic", "Democrat"), ("generic", "Republican")]


def crosstab_table(version_type, version):
    rows_of_version = crosstabs.filter(pl.col("version") == version)
    shares = {(r["variable"], r["group"], r["question"], r["party"]): r["share"]
              for r in rows_of_version.iter_rows(named=True)}
    sizes = {(r["variable"], r["group"]): r["personas"]
             for r in rows_of_version.filter(pl.col("question") == "senate").iter_rows(named=True)}
    body = []
    for variable, (name, order_of_groups) in VARIABLES.items():
        groups = rows_of_version.filter(pl.col("variable") == variable)["group"].unique().to_list()
        if not groups:
            continue
        body.append(f'<tr class="variable"><th colspan="7">{name}</th></tr>')
        for group in in_order(groups, order_of_groups):
            cells = []
            for question, party in COLUMNS:
                share = shares.get((variable, group, question, party))
                cells.append("–" if share is None else f'<span style="color:{colour_of(party)}">{pct(share)}</span>')
            label = STATE_NAMES.get(group, group) if variable == "state" else group
            body.append(f'<tr><td class="indent">{label}</td><td class="num muted">{sizes.get((variable, group), "")}'
                        "</td>" + "".join(f'<td class="num">{c}</td>' for c in cells) + "</tr>")
    head = ('<thead><tr><th></th><th></th><th colspan="3" class="group-head">Senate</th>'
            '<th colspan="2" class="group-head">House</th></tr><tr><th>Group</th><th class="num">Personas</th>'
            '<th class="num">Democrat</th><th class="num">Independent</th><th class="num">Republican</th>'
            '<th class="num">Democrat</th><th class="num">Republican</th></tr></thead>')
    return (f'<table class="plain crosstabs" data-quarto-disable-processing="true">{head}<tbody>{"".join(body)}'
            "</tbody></table>")


show(by_version(crosstab_table))
```

Party ID and ideology tell the most about the answer. On the Senate question, 93% of Strong Democrats chose the Democrat and every Strong Republican chose the Republican. Only the independents split: 40% Democrat, 44% Republican and 15% for an independent candidate. Among other groups, 96% of Black personas chose the Democrat, personas under 45 were more Democratic than older ones (about 56% against 38%), and never-married personas more than married ones (66% against 33%). Women chose the Republican more often than men (54% against 50%). The answers are mostly one-sided within each group, which supports the finding that LLMs flatten people into stereotypes [@bisbee2024].

## Composition of the sample {#composition data-kicker="Composition"}

::: {.how-to-read}
The personas: how many are in each group, and their share of all personas. Every detail here is in the persona's
prompt, except the 2024 vote, which is shown for reference only.
:::

```{python}
#| label: composition
composition = read("persona_composition")
grid = []
for variable, (name, order_of_groups) in VARIABLES.items():
    rows = composition.filter(pl.col("variable") == variable)
    counts = dict(zip(rows["group"], rows["personas"], strict=True))
    total = sum(counts.values())
    grid.append(
        f'<table class="plain small-table" data-quarto-disable-processing="true"><thead><tr><th colspan="2">{name}'
        "</th></tr></thead><tbody>"
        + "".join(f'<tr><td>{STATE_NAMES.get(group, group) if variable == "state" else group}</td>'
                  f'<td class="num">{counts[group]:,} <span class="muted">'
                  f"({pct(counts[group] / total)})</span></td></tr>"
                  for group in in_order(list(counts), order_of_groups))
        + "</tbody></table>"
    )
show('<div class="composition-grid">', *grid, "</div>")
```

The 1,050 personas are real respondents to the 2024 CES. In each of the 35 states with a Senate race, we picked 30 respondents at random. We only picked from respondents who took both parts of the survey (before and after the election) and who answered every question we use in the prompt. The random pick uses a fixed seed, so rerunning the code picks the same 30 people. Each persona's prompt gives their state, age group, gender, race, education, family income, party ID, ideology, religion, marital status, sexual orientation and whether they are registered to vote. Their 2024 vote is not in the prompt; it is shown here only to describe the sample.

Each state has 30 personas, but they may not be representative of the people in that state. Across all states, the sample is older (34% are 65 or over, 7% are under 30) and whiter (80% white) than the country. The forecast corrects for this by age group, gender, race, education, party and state, counting each group by its number of voters in each state.

## Models {#models data-kicker="Models"}

::: {.how-to-read}
Each approach's models, as OpenRouter names them, how they were asked, and what came back. A decision model gives a
probability for each option and each draw is a random pick from them, so it has no temperature.
:::

```{python}
#| label: models
show(table(
    ["Approach", "Model", "Kind", "Draws", "Temperature", "Wording", "Personas", "Answers", "Missing"],
    [[r["approach"].title(), model_name(r["model"]), r["kind"], r["draws"],
      "none" if r["temperature"] is None else f'{r["temperature"]:g}', r["wording"], f'{r["personas"]:,}',
      f'{r["answers"]:,}', f'{r["missing"]:,}'] for r in models.iter_rows(named=True)],
    numeric_from=3,
))
```

For Furkan's approach, we chose two different kinds of model. Jev 1.14 (`typesafe/jev-1.14`) is a decision model: it does not write text, but gives a probability for each answer option, and each of its draws is a random pick from them. We chose it for two reasons. First, because it gives every option a probability, each option is weighed on its own, instead of the model writing out one answer. Second, it is what its makers call a "System One" model, after the fast, intuitive thinking in Kahneman's [*Thinking, Fast and Slow*](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374533557/thinkingfastandslow): its answer is close to a person's quick, intuitive choice, without reasoning. We wanted to see how much the chat models add on top of that, since a fast decision model could give a cheap first picture of a population. It was the cheapest model per call ($0.48 for 21,300 calls), so we took 10 draws per persona and question. Kimi K3 (Moonshot AI) is a chat model, asked 3 times at a temperature of 1.0, like Sean's models. We chose it to see how an advanced Chinese model does on a US election; at $11.39, it was our most expensive model.


For the choice of the Anthropic and Cohere models, 15 different models from 10 companies (Anthropic, Cohere, OpenAI, Google, Meta, Mistral, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Qwen and Z.ai, all different from Furkan's choices) were tested on 25 personas, in both question wordings and with 3 draws each, for a total cost of $0.49. Two could not be run: one because its only provider trains on the prompts it gets, which our settings block, and one because its provider did not accept the requested answer format. Of the remaining 13, Claude Haiku 5.5 (Anthropic) and Command A+ (Cohere 🍁) were selected because they answered 100% of the time, about 90% of the Democratic and Republican personas chose their own party's candidate, and the 3 draws gave the same answer 86% to 94% of the time. Command A+ was one of the most expensive models tested, at about $4 for a full run in the trial's estimate, when most cost under $1. We chose Cohere 🍁 because it is Canadian, and were willing to pay more for the largest of its three models tested, since it was still well within our budget.

## Costs {#costs data-kicker="Costs"}

```{python}
#| label: costs
costs = read("costs").sort("approach", pl.col("model") == "all models", "model")
tokens = {r["model"]: r for r in models.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(table(
    ["Approach", "Model", "Calls", "Personas", "Input tokens", "Output tokens", "Cost", "Cost per persona", "Run on"],
    [[r["approach"].title(), f'<b>{r["model"]}</b>' if r["model"] == "all models" else model_name(r["model"]), f'{r["calls"]:,}',
      f'{r["personas"]:,}',
      f'{tokens[r["model"]]["input_tokens"]:,}' if r["model"] in tokens else "",
      f'{tokens[r["model"]]["output_tokens"]:,}' if r["model"] in tokens else "",
      f'${r["total_cost"]:.2f}', f'${r["cost_per_persona"]:.4f}', r["run_at"][:10]]
     for r in costs.iter_rows(named=True)], numeric_from=2,
))
```

The costs for the four models ranged from $0.41 for Claude Haiku 5.5 to $11.39 for Kimi K3, each of which simulated responses for 1,050 personas, and the whole forecast cost $15.79. Since the models can be run in parallel, the total time is limited by the slowest time of 5 hours (Cohere, Command A+ 🍁). A recent estimate to poll a real voter for a US election is about $50 online to $100 by phone [@gainey2024], which would be $52,500 to $105,000 to poll 1,050 people. Polling would cost about 3,300 to 6,600 times as much as our forecast. However, this may be a case of "you get what you pay for": the election on November 3 will show whether silicon sampling can predict elections accurately for a fraction of the cost of polling.

## Methods {#methods data-kicker="Methods"}

### Data

The personas come from the 2024 Cooperative Election Study [@ces2024], a large survey of American adults before and after the 2024 election. Its validated voters, respondents matched to a record of voting, also give the number of voters in each group. The 2022 CES [@ces2022] gives the same for the 2022 midterm, used only to check how much the forecast depends on whose turnout it uses. Each CES answer is stored as a code, and every code was turned into its label from the CES guide.

The candidates come from Wikipedia's page on the 2026 Senate elections [@wikipedia_senate]: every Democrat and Republican, plus the four main independents (Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and South Dakota). Minor-party candidates are left out, though personas can still answer "Other". In Alaska, which uses ranked-choice voting, the forecast uses the likely final round, the Democrat against the incumbent. Past results come from the MIT Election Data and Science Lab [@mit_senate; @mit_president]: the last Senate election for each seat and the 2024 presidential election, as shares of all votes. Wyoming's two 2020 candidates are both labelled "Other" in the data, so we gave them their parties.

The polls come from VoteHub [@votehub]: `{python} f"{poll_table['poll_id'].n_unique():,}"` general-election polls by `{python} poll_table['pollster'].n_unique()` pollsters in `{python} poll_table['state'].n_unique()` states, kept only if they ask about all of our candidates, so early polls of other possible nominees are left out. Polymarket [@polymarket] gives each race's "Senate Election Winner" market and its daily prices. Candidates' names were matched across the sources by hand where they are written differently (Alaska has two Dan Sullivans). Every cleaned file is checked against its schema with pandera [@pandera] before it is saved. The polls and Polymarket prices are downloaded again every evening until the website is frozen on November 2.

### The silicon sample

Each persona is described to the model in a system message: "You are taking part in a survey of American voters. Answer every question as the person described below would, based on who they are.", followed by one line for each of their details (see [Composition](#composition)). The model is then asked the Senate question with the race's real candidates: "The election for US Senate in [state] is on 3 November 2026. The candidates on your ballot are: [candidates]. Who will you vote for? If you have not decided, answer 'Undecided'. If you will not vote, answer 'Would not vote'." It is also asked the House question, a generic ballot (Democrat, Republican or Other) used as a benchmark, and Alaska's personas are also asked about the final round of its ranked-choice vote. Each question is its own call, and the answer must be one of the options (from a chat model, as JSON), so every answer can be read. The models were queried through OpenRouter [@openrouter].

We each ran our own approach on all 1,050 personas, with the same prompt and questions. Sean's approach used Command A+ 🍁 (Cohere) and Claude Haiku 5.5 (Anthropic), and Furkan's used Jev 1.14 (TypeSafe) and Kimi K3 (Moonshot AI), so the four models come from four different companies. The chat models (all but Jev 1.14) were asked each question 3 times at a temperature of 1.0, so a persona's answers can differ from draw to draw. Jev 1.14, a decision model, was asked 10 times, each answer a random pick from its probabilities. In all, the forecast took 40,470 answers.

### From answers to a forecast

The forecast uses multilevel regression and post-stratification (MRP).

**The model.** Each answer for a candidate is a choice among the parties on the persona's ballot (Democrat, Republican and, in four states, an independent), predicted from the persona's age group, gender, race, education, party (Democrat, Republican, or independent and other) and state, in a multinomial logistic regression. Undecided, would-not-vote and missing answers are left out. The answers of all four models are pooled into one model, and each persona's draws from one model share a weight of 1, so every model counts equally. Every group's effect has a normal prior centred on 0 with a standard deviation of 1 (on the log-odds scale), so a group with few personas is pulled towards the average.

**The frame.** The 2024 CES's validated voters, with their CES weights, give each state's share of voters in every combination of age group, gender, race, education and party, scaled to the state's number of votes for President in 2024.

**Post-stratification.** The model predicts each combination's choice, and each state's vote shares are these predictions weighted by the number of voters in each combination.

**The simulation.** We then simulate the election 10,000 times, to allow for our forecast being wrong. In each simulated election, every state's result is shifted by two random errors. The first is a national error, the same for every state, because forecasts tend to miss in the same direction everywhere. The second is a state error, different for each state. Typically, the national error is within 3 points and the state error within 4.5 points (their standard deviations). Each error moves votes between the Republican and the other candidates: for example, an error of 2 points takes 2 points from the Republican and gives them to the others.

The candidate with the highest share wins; an independent who wins joins the Democrats with a probability of 60% to 80%, by state. Only 35 of the 100 Senate seats are up this year. The other 65 are already decided: 34 are held by Democrats or independents who vote with them, and 31 by Republicans. So in each simulated election, we add the seats each side wins to these 34 and 31. The Democrats need 51 seats to control the Senate; at 50-50, the Vice President, a Republican, breaks the tie.

### Uncertainty

Our forecast has two kinds of uncertainty. The first is the model's own: with 30 personas per state, its coefficients are not known exactly. We approximate their uncertainty with a normal distribution around the most likely coefficients (a Laplace approximation), post-stratify 1,000 draws of them, and take the standard deviation of each state's leading share; the typical (median) state's is 2.0%.

The second is the possible polling error, the error of the method itself. Even a well-estimated forecast can miss the real result: some voters change their minds before election day, and the people who turn out to vote may differ from those we expected. Silicon sampling has no past elections to check how far off it can be, so we assume errors of the size election forecasts usually make: a few points in each state, often in the same direction everywhere. We chose 4 points for each state and 3 points for the whole country. Combined with the model's own 2 points, the error in each state is about 4.5 points.

Each of our 95% intervals covers the middle 95% of the 10,000 simulated elections, and a chance of winning is the share of simulated elections a candidate wins. The polls' 95% interval only shows how much the polls disagree with each other.

## Discussion {#discussion data-kicker="Discussion"}

Our silicon sampling method gives the Democrats only a `{python} pct(combined['dem_control'])` chance of taking control of the Senate, while all the comparisons (polls, betting markets, professional forecasters) give the Democrats between a `{python} pct(min(other_forecasts.values()))` and `{python} pct(max(other_forecasts.values()))` chance. Is our method picking up something all the others are missing, or is our method just not reliable enough? One reason to doubt our method is that our four LLMs disagree on the odds, from `{python} pct(lowest_model['dem_control'])` (`{python} short_version('model', lowest_model['version'])`) to `{python} pct(highest_model['dem_control'])` (`{python} short_version('model', highest_model['version'])`). Note that the combined forecast is not simply the average of the four models' predictions; rather, the answers are pooled before the MRP (see the [Methods](#from-answers-to-a-forecast) section).

All of these forecasts are uncertain. Our `{python} pct(combined['dem_control'])` chance is not far from a coin flip, and 95% of our simulations had between `{python} int(combined['seats_lower'])` and `{python} int(combined['seats_upper'])` Democratic seats. Most of that uncertainty comes from the possible polling error of `{python} pct(combined['polling_state_error_sd'])` in each state, not the models' own uncertainty of `{python} pct(combined['model_standard_error'], 1)`. Silver Bulletin's `{python} pct(other_forecasts['silver_bulletin'])` still gives the Republicans about a `{python} one_in(1 - other_forecasts['silver_bulletin'])` chance of keeping the Senate, and its seat distribution, like ours, spreads across several seats on both sides of 50 [@silver_senate]. One election cannot prove which forecast was better: a `{python} pct(1 - other_forecasts['silver_bulletin'])` or `{python} pct(combined['dem_control'])` chance happens often. The results of all 35 races on November 3 will be a better test than control alone.

In particular, our predictions differ from both the polls and the betting market in four states: Texas, Alaska, Georgia and Michigan (see [Race by race](#races)). We give the Republican only a 52% to 61% chance of winning in each of them, so they are close races for us too. If the Democrats win three of these four and every other race goes as we predict, they would have 51 seats and control of the Senate, which is what the polls and the betting market are predicting. If they win all four, they would have 52 seats, the average in the Silver Bulletin forecast [@silver_senate].

If the silicon sampling turns out to be inaccurate when compared to the election results, there are three plausible explanations. The first is that we did not include any news or current political climate in our prompts, and the models selected may not have been trained with recent information. In contrast, the other forecasts do take into account Trump's low popularity ratings [@silver_approval] and issues that voters have said are important, like corruption and the price of gas and groceries [@cnbc2026]. A second cause is that we are using turnout from the 2024 presidential election, which had high Republican turnout and was not a midterm election. We also ran the simulation using 2022 turnout [@ces2022], the most recent midterm election, but it did not significantly change the prediction: the Democrats' chance of control went from `{python} pct(turnout_control[2024])` to `{python} pct(turnout_control[2022])`. The last midterm election when a Republican was president was 2018, but we decided this election was too old to use. The third plausible explanation is that LLMs may simply not be good predictors of how people vote. @argyle2023 found that GPT-3 could reproduce how groups of Americans voted, which they called "algorithmic fidelity", and in our trial about 90% of the Democratic and Republican personas chose their own party's candidate. However, more recent work finds that LLMs tend to flatten people into stereotypes [@bisbee2024; @wang2024]. We think of each answer as a stereotype with a little noise added: in our trial, the three draws gave the same answer 86% to 94% of the time, and @bisbee2024 also found that the answers change with the model, as ours do.

The big advantage of silicon sampling is that it is much cheaper than polling. On the other hand, betting market prices are free to read, and markets have often predicted elections better than polls [@wolfers2004], so they may turn out to be a better and cheaper alternative to silicon sampling. The election on November 3 will be the first real test of our method against both polling and betting markets.

### Limitations

The choices we made while building our method mean some things were left out or limited, and these could be added or enhanced in future work to check their impact. These limitations are the lack of current news, our choice of low- and mid-priced models, and our decision to try only two wordings of the prompt.

The first limitation is that the prompts were not given any information about the current political climate, which might have shifted the responses. However, even by adding recent news and information about the political climate, we would still have to decide which news sources, what types of news to include, and if each persona should get the same news or different news to reflect their political leaning. @murray2026 found that the news given to the model changed the Democratic share by about 10 percentage points, but had little effect when the persona included political identity, as ours do with party ID. All of these could be important factors, and testing all of them would be considerably more expensive in LLM costs.

A second limitation is that we used models that were either cheap or moderate in price. More expensive models may have more accurate results, either because their training data is more recent or because they are better at detecting voting pattern changes from election to election. Our main reason for not choosing more expensive models was price. We asked the two most expensive models on OpenRouter the same Senate question three times, and estimated that one full run of our approach (`{python} f"{full_run_calls:,}"` calls) would cost about `{python} f"${round(full_run_cost['openai/gpt-5.5-pro'], -3):,.0f}"` for GPT-5.5 Pro and `{python} f"${full_run_cost['anthropic/claude-fable-5.1']:,.0f}"` for Claude Fable 5.1, against `{python} f"${run_cost['moonshotai/kimi-k3']:,.0f}"` for Kimi K3 and `{python} f"${full_run_cost['cohere/command-a-plus']:,.2f}"` for Cohere's Command A+ 🍁.

The final limitation that could be addressed with future work is varying the prompt. @heath2026 found that asking for political opinions in the model's own words, then mapping the text to a numeric scale, gives distributions of answers that more closely fit real respondents' than asking for a number. Different prompts could be tested to get better distributions of votes, which might lead to more accurate predictions.

As @murray2026 found, the choice of model, persona detail, news and prompt style together could move the Democratic share anywhere from 0 to 100%, so any change to the method should be checked against real election results. We will wait for the results on November 3, 2026 before trying any of these changes, so we can first see how accurate the current method is.

### References

The analysis was done in Python [@python] with polars [@polars], NumPy [@numpy], SciPy [@scipy], pandera [@pandera], the OpenAI Python library [@openai_python] and pytest [@pytest]. The models were queried through OpenRouter [@openrouter], and the website was built with Quarto [@quarto] and Plotly [@plotly]. The data come from the CES [@ces2024; @ces2022], the MIT Election Lab [@mit_senate; @mit_president], Wikipedia [@wikipedia_senate], VoteHub [@votehub] and Polymarket [@polymarket].

```{=html}
<script>
// Menus and buttons that show one view at a time (made by choices() in src/senate_forecast_2026/website.py). A
// menu and the views it switches share a name; several groups of views can share one menu (the version menu).
function showChoice(name, value) {
  document.querySelectorAll(`[data-choice-view="${name}"]`).forEach(view => {
    view.hidden = view.dataset.value !== value;
    if (!view.hidden && window.Plotly) view.querySelectorAll(".js-plotly-plot").forEach(p => Plotly.Plots.resize(p));
  });
  document.querySelectorAll(`select[data-choice="${name}"]`).forEach(s => s.value = value);
  document.querySelectorAll(`button[data-choice="${name}"]`).forEach(b => b.classList.toggle("active", b.dataset.value === value));
}
document.querySelectorAll("select[data-choice]").forEach(s => s.addEventListener("change", () => showChoice(s.dataset.choice, s.value)));
document.querySelectorAll("button[data-choice]").forEach(b => b.addEventListener("click", () => showChoice(b.dataset.choice, b.dataset.value)));
</script>
```
